title: Until the Lion Learns to Write
proverb: Until the lion learns to write, every story will glorify the hunter.
literal_meaning: If only the hunter is the one who tells the story, the lion will always be described as the defeated animal and the hunter as the hero.
deeper_meaning: History is often written by those who have power, education, or the opportunity to tell their side. Until everyone has the ability to record and share their own experiences, many voices and perspectives may remain forgotten.
historical_background: The Ewe people, like many African communities, preserved knowledge through oral traditions. Elders, storytellers, and historians passed down accounts of battles, migrations, leadership, and community experiences through spoken stories. This proverb became a reminder that storytelling is connected to power and that every group deserves the chance to preserve its own history.
cultural_significance: Among African societies, storytelling is not only entertainment; it is a way of protecting identity, culture, and memory. The proverb teaches younger generations to learn, write, document, and share their own history instead of allowing others to define them completely.

story.title: The Lion Who Wanted His Voice Heard
story.content:
Long ago, in a great forest, there lived many animals. Every year, the animals gathered to hear stories about the past. The hunter was the only one who knew how to write, so he recorded all the events that happened in the forest.

Whenever the hunter wrote about a meeting with the lion, the story always ended the same way: the hunter was brave, and the lion was defeated.

The other animals listened and believed the stories because no one else could write.

One day, the lion gathered the animals and asked, 'Did anyone ever ask me what happened during those encounters?'

The animals became silent. They realized that they had only heard one side of every story.

The lion said, 'The hunter is not wrong to tell his story, but the forest is incomplete when only one voice is heard.'

Years passed, and the young animals began learning how to write. The lion's children, the birds, and other creatures started recording their own experiences.

When the new stories were shared, the animals discovered that every event had many sides. The hunter had his courage, but the lion also had his strength and wisdom.

The elders then said, 'Until the lion learns to write, the hunter will always appear as the greatest hero.'

life_lessons: Everyone deserves the chance to tell their own story.
A community that does not record its history may lose it.
modern_application: The proverb encourages communities to document their languages, traditions, experiences, and achievements. In the modern world, people use books, technology, journalism, and digital platforms to preserve their own stories.
